parts.label: a
hints: For the discrete event $X \le 45$, the bar representing 45 extends from $44.5$ to $45.5$. To include 45, take $Y < 45.5$.
Standardise using $z = \frac{y - \mu}{\sigma} = \frac{45.5 - 40}{\sqrt{24}}$ and look up $\Phi(z)$.

walkthrough.text:
Apply the continuity correction for an upper cumulative bound $X \le k$:
$$\text{P}(X \le 45) \approx \text{P}(Y < 45.5)$$

Standardise the continuous variable $Y$ using $\mu = 40$ and $\sigma = \sqrt{24}$:
$$z = \frac{45.5 - 40}{\sqrt{24}} = \frac{5.5}{4.89898} \approx 1.123$$
$$\text{P}(Y < 45.5) = \Phi(1.123) \approx 0.869$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
The discrete bar for 45 covers the interval $[44.5, 45.5]$. Because $X \le 45$ includes 45, we integrate up to the upper boundary:
$$\text{P}(X \le 45) \approx \text{P}(Y < 45.5)$$

Calculate the standard score and read the standard normal cumulative table:
$$z = \frac{45.5 - 40}{\sqrt{24}} \approx 1.123$$
$$\Phi(1.123) = 0.869$$

ai_rubric.observable: Apply continuity correction to rewrite P(X <= 45) as P(Y < 45.5) and standardise with (45.5 - 40)/sqrt(24).
Obtain z = 1.123 and evaluate Phi(1.123) = 0.869.

parts.label: a
hints: Note the strict inequality: $X < 26$ is equivalent to $X \le 25$ for integer values.

walkthrough.text:
Convert the strict inequality to an inclusive discrete inequality:
$$X < 26 \iff X \le 25$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:

parts.label: a

$$\text{Discrete event:} \quad X \le 49$$

The continuous boundary enclosing 49 is $49.5$:
$$\text{Continuous event:} \quad Y < 49.5$$

parts.label: a
hints: 'Between 50 and 70 inclusive' corresponds to the discrete range $50 \le X \le 70$.

walkthrough.text:
Identify the discrete inequality for 'between 50 and 70 inclusive':
$$50 \le X \le 70$$

Evaluate using table values:
$$2(0.9599) - 1 = 0.9198$$

parts.label: a
hints: For a single throw of three 4-sided dice, each die shows a 1 with probability $\frac{1}{4}$ and does not show a 1 with probability $\frac{3}{4}$.
At least two dice showing a 1 corresponds to exactly 2 dice showing a 1 or all 3 dice showing a 1.
Use the binomial formula: $\text{P}(\text{exactly 2}) = \binom{3}{2}\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^2\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^1$.
Add $\text{P}(\text{all 3}) = \binom{3}{3}\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^3$ and simplify the fraction.

walkthrough.text:
Calculate the probability of obtaining exactly two 1s on three dice:
$$\text{P}(\text{two 1s}) = \binom{3}{2} \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^2 \left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^1 = 3 \times \frac{1}{16} \times \frac{3}{4} = \frac{9}{64}$$
Calculate the probability of obtaining all three 1s:
$$\text{P}(\text{three 1s}) = \binom{3}{3} \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^3 = 1 \times \frac{1}{64} = \frac{1}{64}$$

Add the mutually exclusive probabilities:
$$p = \frac{9}{64} + \frac{1}{64} = \frac{10}{64} = \frac{5}{32}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Let $W$ be the number of 1s in a single throw, where $W \sim \text{B}\left(3, \frac{1}{4}\right)$:
$$\text{P}(W \ge 2) = \text{P}(W = 2) + \text{P}(W = 3)$$
$$\text{P}(W = 2) = 3\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^2\left(\frac{3}{4}\right) = \frac{9}{64}, \quad \text{P}(W = 3) = \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^3 = \frac{1}{64}$$

Combine both probabilities to confirm the result:
$$p = \frac{9}{64} + \frac{1}{64} = \frac{10}{64} = \frac{5}{32}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Calculate probabilities of exactly 2 ones (3*(1/4)^2*(3/4) = 9/64) and exactly 3 ones ((1/4)^3 = 1/64).
Sum the two probabilities: 9/64 + 1/64 = 10/64 = 5/32.

parts.label: b
hints: Calculate expected successes $np = 128 \times \frac{5}{32}$ and expected failures $nq = 128 \times \frac{27}{32}$.

Compute the mean $\mu = np$ and variance $\sigma^2 = npq$.
State the approximating normal model $Y \sim \text{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$.

walkthrough.text:
Calculate expected successes and failures:
$$np = 128 \times \frac{5}{32} = 20, \quad nq = 128 \times \frac{27}{32} = 108$$

Check the validity conditions:
$$np = 20 > 5 \quad \text{and} \quad nq = 108 > 5$$
Since both conditions are satisfied, a normal approximation is valid.

Find the variance and state the distribution of $Y$:
$$\sigma^2 = npq = 20 \times \frac{27}{32} = 16.875$$
$$Y \sim \text{N}(20, 16.875)$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Evaluate expected counts:
$$np = 128\left(\frac{5}{32}\right) = 20, \quad nq = 128\left(\frac{27}{32}\right) = 108$$

Verify validity criteria:
$$20 > 5 \quad \text{and} \quad 108 > 5 \implies \text{Normal approximation is justified}$$

Calculate parameters and specify model:
$$\mu = 20, \quad \sigma^2 = 128\left(\frac{5}{32}\right)\left(\frac{27}{32}\right) = 16.875$$
$$Y \sim \text{N}(20, 16.875)$$

ai_rubric.observable: State that both np = 20 > 5 and nq = 108 > 5, confirming the normal approximation is valid.
Calculate variance sigma^2 = 128 * (5/32) * (27/32) = 16.875 and state Y ~ N(20, 16.875).

teacher_walkthrough.text:

Standardise the value:

parts.label: a
hints: Calculate expected successes $np = 200 \times 0.6$ and expected failures $nq = 200 \times 0.4$.

parts.label: c
hints: Notice that strictly more than 135 heads means $X > 135$, so 135 is excluded and values start at 136 ($X \ge 136$).
The boundary between 135 and 136 is $135.5$, giving the continuous event $Y > 135.5$.
Standardise $Y = 135.5$ using $\mu = 120$ and $\sigma = \sqrt{48}$.
Compute the upper tail probability $1 - \Phi(z)$.

walkthrough.text:
Convert the strict inequality and apply the continuity correction:
$$X > 135 \iff X \ge 136 \implies \text{P}(X > 135) \approx \text{P}(Y > 135.5)$$

Standardise $Y = 135.5$ using $\mu = 120$ and $\sigma = \sqrt{48}$:
$$z = \frac{135.5 - 120}{\sqrt{48}} = \frac{15.5}{6.9282} \approx 2.237$$

Evaluate the upper tail probability:
$$\text{P}(Y > 135.5) = 1 - \Phi(2.237) = 1 - 0.9874 = 0.0126$$
